title: Profiling snapshot orchestration notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a living engineering note describing an operational pattern for orchestrating profiling snapshots during performance alerts and regression hunts. It focuses on: (1) reproducible snapshot capture, (2) side-by-side metric and trace diffs for canary vs baseline, (3) structured bisect steps that reduce blast radius, and (4) quick escalation and rollback play.

When to use this doc:
- Alert fires for sustained increase in p95/p99 latency, tail token stalls, or throughput degradation.
- Canary shows divergence between two deployments or model variants.
- We need reproducible artifacts for post-mortem and model-team rollback decisions.

High-level flow (one-line):
1) snapshot capture, 2) baseline/canary alignment, 3) triage queries & short hypothesis list, 4) staged bisect, 5) mitigation and capture artifacts for post-mortem.

Snapshot capture (quick):
- Purpose: freeze state so metric/trace/profile diffs are stable while we investigate.
- What to capture:
  - short flamegraph (5–20s) from runtime profiler (async sampler)
  - KV-cache hit histograms and eviction traces (last 5 minutes)
  - Per-instance latency distribution (per route/model/pod)
  - Prometheus/metrics scrape range (t-15m..t+2m) compressed
  - Example request bundles (masked PII) that reproduce slow path
  - System-level counters (GPU utilization, memory allocs, page-faults)

- Automated snapshot endpoint (internal):
  curl -X POST "https://internal-api.redwood/profiler/snapshot?job=triage&duration_s=20" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
  Response: JSON with artifact URLs (flame.tar.gz, traces.pb, metrics.tar.gz)

Guidelines for sample bundles:
- Capture 50–200 requests representative of the traffic that triggered the alert. Keep seeds for deterministic prompts (same token lengths).
- Include both short (<64 tokens) and long (>512 tokens) samples if alert correlates with sequence length.

Dashboards and quick queries (starter PromQL/Datadog):
- p95 latency across routes: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- Token-generation tail latency (per-model): sum(rate(token_generation_latency_sum[1m])) / sum(rate(token_generation_latency_count[1m])) by (model)
- KV cache hit ratio: 1 - sum(kv_cache_misses_total[5m]) / sum(kv_cache_requests_total[5m])
- Active batch size distribution: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(batch_size_bucket[5m]))
- Compare canary vs baseline using split by deployment tag in the same graph. If using Datadog, use group_by([deployment]) and overlay.

Trace diffs (what to look for):
- Growing time in attention/decoder kernels vs steady encode time.
- Increased time spent in RPC orchestration (grpc queue time) even if kernel time stable => suspect batching/queue pressure.
- Spikes in GPU memcpy or page-faults indicate memory pressure/eviction.

Bisect strategy (safe, low-blast):
- Goal: identify change that explains regression with minimal rollbacks.
- Prefer feature-flag toggles, model pinning, or instance-level kills over cluster-wide rollback.
- Example steps: 
  1) Narrow to model or infra: switch traffic on a small sample (1–5%) to a pinned baseline model for 30 minutes. If tail latency reverts, model change is likely.
  2) If model not implicated, toggle runtime feature flags (e.g., adaptive-batching=false) on a single AZ and observe.
  3) Commit incremental rollbacks: model weight -> quantization profile -> batching heuristic -> kernel selection order. Test after each step for 15–30m.
  4) If suspect commit range exists, do git bisect of the serving runtime repo but run bisect tests against a synthetic load harness that reproduces the tail behavior.

Bisect commands (example harness):
  # run synthetic harness against candidate commit
  ./tools/load-test/run.sh --commit $SHA --concurrency 100 --seq-dist small:0.6,medium:0.3,long:0.1 --duration 600 --capture-artifacts /tmp/artifacts/$SHA

Canary vs baseline comparison checklist:
- Use identical input bundles for both sides.
- Align sampling windows: compare t0..t0+10m for both deployments, not arbitrary ranges.
- Normalize for traffic rate differences: look at per-request or per-token metrics, not aggregate counts.
- Capture per-bucket batch size heatmaps — shifts in batch distribution change per-token cost and latency.

Common root causes and investigative signals:
- KV cache regression: rising cold-start latency, eviction rate up — check cache occupancy and recent config changes.
- Batching regression: average batch size drops or batch variance increases — suspect scheduler change or bursty upstream.
- Kernel regression: per-kernel op time rises with no change in queueing — suspect compiled kernel selection or BLAS change.
- Memory pressure: OOM kills, GPU page faults, or frequent memcpy spikes.

Quick mitigation options (first hour):
- Fail open to a cheaper/older model variant for non-essential traffic.
- Disable adaptive batching or reduce max batch size temporarily.
- Shift traffic to alternative region/cluster with different kernel/config.
- Throttle low-priority routes via rate limits and focus capacity on high-SLA routes.

Escalation & handoff notes:
- If rollback or toggle fixes the issue, capture the following for post-mortem: snapshot artifacts, diff graphs (p95/p99), exact deploy IDs, and the set of inputs used. Attach to the incident in Linear (linked_artifacts above).
- Owner: person who acknowledged alert remains responsible for artifact capture. If unclear, default to on-call engineer from eng-serving-runtime.

Post-mortem checklist (for the owner):
- Timeline (when did metric change start, detect, respond, and mitigate)
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence (metric diffs, flamegraphs, commits)
- Actions taken (rollbacks, toggles, config patches)
- Follow-ups (tests to add, alert threshold tuning, slow-path unit test to cover scenario)

Open items / TODOs:
- Add an automated job to snapshot the current canary every 5m during a flagged rollout (ticket: RUN-3919).
- Build a small UI in Console that overlays baseline vs canary flamegraphs for quick eyeballing.
- Add a synthetic tail-load test for bisect harness that reproduces token-stall patterns.

Appendix: useful quick links & commands
- Artifact store: https://artifacts.redwood/internal/profiler
- Canary toggle CLI: rctl rollout toggle --deployment $NAME --tag canary --pct 1
- Fetch flamegraph: curl -s $ARTIFACT_URL | tar -xzO > /tmp/flame.svg
- Example PromQL for devs: rate(request_latency_bucket{route=~"/generate.*",deployment=~"(baseline|canary)"}[5m])

Notes/voice: this is intentionally terse and operational — meant for the on-call detective who needs reproducible artifacts fast. Keep it updated as we discover new recurring signals.
